summary_html: A **judge orders** CPS to investigate or assess during civil/criminal proceedings. Federal funding statutes (ASFA/IV-E) tether court findings to child-welfare actions, embedding judicial oversight into intake-to-case flow.
authority_html:
- **ASFA (42 U.S.C. §§ 671–675)** — court ‘reasonable efforts’ findings; permanency timelines  
- **SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — funding structure linking court oversight to agency actions

primary_citations.citation_text: Iowa - Title VI, Chapter 232 (Juvenile Justice – includes mandatory reporting and child in need of assistance)

regulations_applicable.title: Agency 249 - EARLY CHILDHOOD IOWA STATE BOARD
Agency 428 - Criminal And Juvenile Justice Planning Division

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: Reversing a dismissal, the court held that the 'court's aid is not required' ground for dismissal in Iowa Code section 232.96(8) must be construed narrowly; in reaching that result it relied on the legislature's two-stage adjudication/disposition structure, under which the juvenile court may make no disposition until the court-directed social investigation under section 232.97 has been completed and a report submitted, and under which a physical and mental examination may also be ordered under section 232.98 to aid the court at disposition.
key_cases.relevance: This is the Iowa Supreme Court's own statement of the rule that a judicially directed investigation by the department (Iowa Code section 232.97) is a mandatory predicate to juvenile-court disposition, which is the principal Iowa mechanism by which a judge orders the child-welfare agency to investigate during a pending case.
key_cases.quote: the court is not allowed to make any disposition until a social investigation has been completed and a report submitted to the court

key_cases.case_name: In re the Marriage of Reschly
key_cases.holding: Affirming an award of custody to the maternal grandparents, the court held that the written report of a court-ordered investigation by a psychiatrist was hearsay that should have been excluded and should not have been considered at any stage, because the statutory route for admitting such a report (Iowa Code section 232.96(6)) is confined to child-in-need-of-assistance proceedings and no other exception (section 598A.19 or section 622.28) applied; the court declined to consider the report's substance.
key_cases.relevance: At INP-04 it establishes that the product of a court-ordered investigation carries no automatic evidentiary status outside a CINA case, so a judge's referral in a dissolution or other civil proceeding does not make the resulting report admissible.
key_cases.quote: Dr. Jenkins’ report is not admissible under Iowa Code section 232.96(6) because this is not a child in need of assistance proceeding

key_cases.case_name: In the Interest of J.B., Minor Child
key_cases.holding: Affirming adjudication and disposition, the court held the father failed to preserve his challenge to the juvenile court's use of the department's social-investigation report, and held in the alternative that Iowa Code section 232.97(1) does not require an express parental waiver of the five-working-day period between filing of the social report and disposition; the court may waive that period on the agreement of all the parties, which the hearing transcript showed.
key_cases.relevance: It supplies the procedural rules that attach to the court-ordered social investigation at INP-04 — the five-day report-consideration period, how it may be waived, and the need to object contemporaneously to preserve any challenge.
key_cases.quote: Even if the father had preserved error, section 232.97 does not require an express waiver by the parents

key_cases.case_name: In the Interest of J.R., D.R., and H.R., Minor Children
key_cases.holding: Affirming a permanency order, the court held that the father's claim that the district court entered a dispositional order without a section 232.97 social investigation and report was waived because he did not appeal the dispositional order, and that counsel was not ineffective for failing to press the point: although the record showed no social investigation report was ever prepared, the caseworker testified he had learned the same background information from other sources, so there was no Strickland prejudice.
key_cases.relevance: It answers the practical question at INP-04 of what follows when the court-ordered investigation is never performed — in Iowa the omission is condemned but is not itself reversible absent a preserved objection and demonstrated prejudice.
key_cases.quote: We do not condone the department’s failure to comply with section 232.97

key_cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Des Moines detectives conducting a child welfare check were not entitled to qualified immunity for arresting a mother on her porch after she refused their demands: without a warrant, an exigency, a removal order, or her consent, they could neither enter the home nor compel her to produce the child.
key_cases.relevance: It identifies the judicial order as the constitutionally lawful route when a parent refuses access during an Iowa assessment, which is the operative federal constraint on the court-order pathway contemplated by Iowa Code section 232.71B(6) at INP-04.
key_cases.quote: they could not lawfully enter the home without Webster's consent, nor force her to take any specific action with respect to L.B.

key_cases.case_name: In the Interest of J.A. (Racine County v. Skow)
key_cases.holding: Reversing the court of appeals, the court held that a judge assigned to exercise jurisdiction under the Children's Code has statutory power under Wis. Stat. sections 48.08(1), 48.067(9) and 48.069(1)(e) to order the county human services department to make investigations and reports about any problem the judge reasonably believes exists in the foster care program, provided the order is triggered by information received while handling a particular case and the judge states the reasons in the order, which is reviewable for abuse of discretion; the grant of that power does not violate separation of powers.
key_cases.relevance: This is the closest neighboring-state high-court holding squarely on the INP-04 doctrine — the source and outer limits of a juvenile judge's authority to order the child-welfare agency to investigate and report — a question Iowa's appellate courts have not yet decided.
key_cases.quote: the scope of the social service department's duty to provide information must be coextensive with the judge's duties under the statute

key_cases.case_name: S.M. v. E.M.B.R. (In re Adoption of C.M.B.R.)
key_cases.holding: The court held on plain-error review that the trial court's failure to order and receive the investigations and written reports mandated by Mo. Rev. Stat. sections 211.455, 453.070.1 and 453.077.1 before trial was a manifest injustice requiring reversal of the termination of the mother's parental rights and the adoption decree, and remanded with directions that the court order compliance with those reporting requirements before retrial.
key_cases.relevance: It is the neighboring-state counterpoint to Iowa's harmless-error treatment: where the statute makes a court-ordered agency investigation a precondition to judgment, failure to order it can itself void the result — the live risk a practitioner faces at INP-04.
key_cases.quote: Under section 453.070.1, an adoption decree may not be entered until the juvenile division receives and reviews written reports about the adoptive parents and the child’s suitability for adoption

state_agency.name: Iowa Department of Health and Human Services, Child Protective Services

mandatory_reporters: Health practitioners who examine, attend, or treat a child — § 232.69(1)(a)
Employees/operators of public or private health care facilities — § 232.69(1)(b)(2)
Licensed school employees, certified para-educators, coaching-authorization holders, school employees age 18 or older, and community college instructors — § 232.69(1)(b)(4)

Employees/operators of licensed child care centers, registered child development homes, head start programs, family development and self-sufficiency grant programs, and HOPES–Healthy Families Iowa programs — § 232.69(1)(b)(5)
Employees/operators of licensed substance use disorder programs or facilities — § 232.69(1)(b)(6)
Employees of department institutions listed in Iowa Code § 218.1 — § 232.69(1)(b)(7)
Employees/operators of juvenile detention or juvenile shelter care facilities — § 232.69(1)(b)(8)
Employees/operators of child foster care facilities — § 232.69(1)(b)(9)
Employees/operators of providers of services to children funded under a federally approved medical assistance home and community-based services waiver — § 232.69(1)(b)(13)
Employees, operators, owners, and others who perform duties for certified children's residential facilities — § 232.69(1)(b)(14)
reporting_details: Iowa is a designated-professional reporting state: the classes of persons listed in Iowa Code § 232.69(1) must report suspected child abuse within 24 hours, while any other person may report but is not required to (Iowa Code § 232.69(2)).

timeline_requirements.deadline: 24 hours (child abuse assessment) or 72 hours (family assessment)
20 business days (child abuse assessment); 10 business days (family assessment)
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Receipt of the child abuse report

notice_requirements.timing: Within 5 working days of commencing the assessment (Iowa Code § 232.71B(2)); a court may direct the department to withhold notification if it would endanger the child or other persons

parent_rights_at_moment: Right to refuse entry without warrant
what_to_say: I do not consent to entry without a warrant
Please provide your card and the allegations in writing
I will have my attorney contact you
what_not_to_do: Do not let them in 'just to look'
